q: A respiratory therapist records four observations about a patient. Which one is quantitative?
c: The patient says breathing feels tight.
y: Correct: a number with a unit (here a percent) is a measurement, so it is quantitative.
A color described in words is qualitative; no number is measured.
A patient's description in words is qualitative.
A sound described in words is qualitative.
h: Look for the observation that includes a measured number.
w: Quantitative observations are measurements: a number with a unit. Only "94%" is measured; the others describe qualities in words.

q: A student tests whether temperature changes how fast an antacid tablet dissolves. She drops identical tablets into 200 mL of water at 10 °C, 25 °C and 40 °C and times how long each takes to dissolve. What is the dependent variable?
c: The time it takes the tablet to dissolve
y: Correct: the dissolving time is what she measures, and it depends on the temperature she chose.
Temperature is what she changes on purpose: the independent variable.
The volume is kept the same in every trial: a constant.
The tablets are identical in every trial: a constant.
h: The dependent variable is what you measure, not what you set.
w: She sets the temperature (independent variable), keeps volume and tablet type the same (constants), and measures the dissolving time (dependent variable).

q: Which statement is a scientific law?
c: When ice melts in a closed container, the total mass does not change.
Matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving.
Adding fertilizer to this field will raise the almond yield.
Atoms rearrange during reactions because their electrons are shared or transferred.
y: Correct: it states what always happens, without explaining why. That is a law (conservation of mass).
This explains why matter behaves as it does using a particle model: a theory.
This is an untested prediction about one field: a hypothesis.
This explains why reactions happen: part of a theory, not a law.
h: A law describes WHAT always happens; a theory explains WHY.
w: Laws summarize repeated observations (mass is conserved). Theories explain them with a model (atoms, particles). A single untested prediction is a hypothesis.

q: Which of these is a compound?
y: Correct: NH<sub>3</sub> has two different elements, N and H, bonded in a fixed 1:3 ratio.
N<sub>2</sub> contains only nitrogen atoms; it is a diatomic element.
Air is a homogeneous mixture of gases, not one substance.
Fe is a single element.
h: A compound needs two or more different element symbols bonded in one formula.
w: Only NH<sub>3</sub> contains two different elements bonded together in a fixed ratio. N<sub>2</sub> and Fe are elements; air is a mixture.

q: A bottle of 70% isopropyl alcohol from a clinic supply room is clear and looks the same throughout. How is it classified?
y: Correct: it is isopropyl alcohol and water mixed evenly; the label even tells you the composition can vary (70%, 91%).
Isopropyl alcohol alone is a compound, but this bottle contains alcohol mixed with water.
An element contains only one kind of atom; alcohol and water contain C, H and O.
It looks the same throughout, so it is not heterogeneous.
h: A percent on the label tells you something is mixed with something else.
w: "70%" means 70 parts alcohol per 100 parts total, the rest water. Two substances, evenly mixed, variable composition: a homogeneous mixture (a solution).

q: Which list contains only elements that exist as diatomic molecules?
y: Correct: hydrogen, nitrogen and chlorine are all among the diatomic seven (H, N, O, F, Cl, Br, I).
Helium is a noble gas that exists as single He atoms, not He<sub>2</sub>.
Carbon is not one of the diatomic seven.
Sodium is a metal and is not one of the diatomic seven.
h: The diatomic seven: H, N, O, F, Cl, Br, I.
w: Only H<sub>2</sub>, N<sub>2</sub>, O<sub>2</sub>, F<sub>2</sub>, Cl<sub>2</sub>, Br<sub>2</sub> and I<sub>2</sub> exist as diatomic molecules. He, C and Na do not.

q: A lab technician needs to separate red blood cells from plasma in a blood sample quickly. Which method works best?
y: Correct: spinning the tube forces the denser cells to the bottom and leaves plasma on top.
Distillation separates liquids by boiling point and would destroy the sample.
Ordinary filter paper is not used to separate blood cells from plasma; the cells clog it and the sample is ruined.
Evaporating the water would leave everything dried together, not separated.
h: Which method uses density and works on a small tube of liquid?
w: Centrifugation separates by density. Red blood cells are denser than plasma, so they pack at the bottom of the tube.

q: Which statement correctly compares the particles in liquid water and in water vapor at the same temperature?
c: In the liquid the molecules touch; in the vapor they are far apart.
In the liquid the molecules are locked in fixed positions; in the vapor they slide past each other.
The molecules in the vapor are larger than those in the liquid.
The vapor contains hydrogen and oxygen atoms that are no longer bonded.
y: Correct: liquid particles are close and touching; gas particles are spread far apart.
Locked positions describe a solid, not a liquid. Sliding past each other describes a liquid, not a gas.
The molecules are the same size in every state; only their spacing changes.
Boiling is a physical change: the H<sub>2</sub>O molecules stay intact.
h: Changing state changes spacing and motion, not the molecules themselves.
w: Liquid water: molecules touching but moving past one another. Water vapor: the same H<sub>2</sub>O molecules, far apart and moving fast.

q: A sample is poured from a tall, narrow flask into a wide dish. Its shape changes, but its volume stays 50 mL. What is the sample?
c: Either a gas or a solid
y: Correct: a fixed volume but no fixed shape is the definition of a liquid.
A solid keeps its own shape; it would not spread into the dish.
A gas would expand to fill the whole space it is in, so its volume would change.
Neither fits: a solid keeps its shape and a gas changes its volume.
h: Which state has a definite volume but no definite shape?
w: Liquids take the shape of their container but keep their volume, because the particles touch yet slide past each other.

q: Why can far more oxygen be stored in a steel cylinder as a gas than you might expect from the cylinder's size?
c: Gas particles are mostly empty space apart, so they can be pushed much closer together.
Oxygen molecules shrink when they are compressed.
The oxygen turns into a compound inside the cylinder.
Gas particles stop moving when they are compressed.
y: Correct: compressing a gas removes empty space between particles, so many more fit in the same volume.
Molecules do not change size; only the space between them changes.
Compressing a gas is a physical change; O<sub>2</sub> stays O<sub>2</sub>.
Gas particles keep moving; compression only brings them closer together.
h: Think about how much empty space is in a gas.
w: Gases are compressible because their particles are far apart. Squeezing the gas into a cylinder removes much of that space without changing the molecules.

q: A magnesium ion, Mg<sup>2+</sup>, is placed near a phosphate ion, PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup>. What happens?
c: They neither attract nor repel, because the charges have different sizes.
They repel, because the phosphate charge is larger.
y: Correct: one is positive and one is negative, and opposite charges attract.
Repulsion happens only between like charges (+ with + or − with −).
Different sizes change how strong the force is, not whether there is a force.
The direction depends only on the signs; the sizes change the strength.
h: Look only at the signs to decide attract or repel.
w: Mg<sup>2+</sup> is positive and PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup> is negative, so they attract. Their large charges make the attraction strong; this is part of why magnesium phosphate is a hard solid.

q: Two ion pairs are compared. In pair A, Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> are 0.28 nm apart. In pair B, the same two ions are 0.56 nm apart. Which statement is true?
c: Pair A attracts more strongly, because the ions are closer together.
Pair B attracts more strongly, because there is more space between the ions.
Both pairs attract equally, because the charges are the same.
Pair B repels, because the ions are far apart.
y: Correct: with the same charges, the closer pair feels the stronger attraction.
More distance weakens the force; it does not strengthen it.
Same charges, but different distances; distance changes the strength.
Opposite charges attract at any distance; distance changes only the strength.
h: Same charges, different distances: which pair is closer?
w: The force between charges grows as they get closer. Doubling the distance makes the attraction much weaker, but it is still an attraction.

q: Pulling a Na<sup>+</sup> ion away from a Cl<sup>−</sup> ion that it is touching requires what?
c: An input of energy, because opposite charges attract
Nothing; the ions separate on their own
A release of energy, because the ions repel
A third ion with the same charge as both
y: Correct: opposite charges attract, so separating them takes energy, like pulling two magnets apart.
Opposite charges attract, so they will not drift apart on their own.
Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> attract; they do not repel, and separating them absorbs energy.
No single charge can be the same as both a + and a − ion.
h: Is it easier to pull two attracting magnets apart, or to let them snap together?
w: Separating opposite charges takes energy; letting them come together releases energy. This is why melting salt takes a lot of heat.

q: Which is a chemical change?
c: A cut apple slice turns brown in air.
A sugar cube dissolves in hot tea.
Wet laundry dries on a line.
y: Correct: substances in the apple react with oxygen to form new, brown substances.
Dissolving is physical; evaporating the tea would give back the sugar.
Melting is a change of state, a physical change.
Drying is evaporation, a change of state, a physical change.
h: Ask: did a new substance form?
w: Browning of a cut apple is a reaction between compounds in the fruit and oxygen, forming new colored substances. The other three are physical changes.

q: Which property of copper is a chemical property?
c: It slowly turns green when exposed to moist air for years.
y: Correct: forming a green coating (patina) means copper reacts to make new substances.
Conducting electricity does not change the copper into anything new; it is physical.
A melting point is measured without changing the substance's identity: physical.
Color and shine are observed without changing the copper: physical.
h: A chemical property describes how a substance changes into something new.
w: Copper's slow reaction with air and moisture to form a green patina is a chemical property. Conductivity, melting point and color are physical properties.

q: On a cold morning, water vapor in the air turns directly into frost on a car windshield without first becoming liquid. What is this change called?
y: Correct: deposition is gas → solid.
Sublimation is the reverse, solid → gas.
Condensation is gas → liquid; here no liquid formed.
Freezing is liquid → solid; here there was no liquid.
h: Start state: gas. End state: solid.
w: Gas going straight to solid is deposition. It is a physical change: the water molecules are unchanged.

q: Which property can help identify an unknown liquid because it does not depend on how much liquid you have?
c: Length of the column in the cylinder
y: Correct: boiling point is intensive; a drop and a liter of the same liquid boil at the same temperature.
Mass is extensive; it grows with the amount of sample.
Volume is extensive; it grows with the amount of sample.
The height of liquid in a cylinder depends on how much you pour in: extensive.
h: Intensive properties stay the same for any amount of sample.
w: Intensive properties (boiling point, density, color) do not depend on amount, so they can identify a substance. Extensive properties (mass, volume) depend on how much you have.

q: A 25.0 mL sample of a clear liquid has a mass of 31.5 g. What is its density?
y: Correct: d = m/V = 31.5 g ÷ 25.0 mL = 1.26 g/mL.
This is volume ÷ mass (25.0 ÷ 31.5); the fraction is upside down.
This multiplies mass by volume instead of dividing.
This subtracts the numbers; density is a ratio of mass to volume.
h: Density = mass ÷ volume.
w: d = 31.5 g ÷ 25.0 mL = 1.26 g/mL. (A liquid with this density is denser than water, so it would sink below water if they did not mix.)

q: A metal nugget has a mass of 193 g. When it is dropped into a graduated cylinder, the water level rises from 20.0 mL to 30.0 mL. What is the nugget's density?
y: Correct: the nugget's volume is 30.0 − 20.0 = 10.0 mL, and 193 g ÷ 10.0 mL = 19.3 g/mL (the density of gold).
This divides by the final water level (193 ÷ 30.0); use only the volume change.
This divides by the starting water level (193 ÷ 20.0); use only the volume change.
This divides the volume by the mass (10.0 ÷ 193); density is mass ÷ volume.
h: The nugget's volume is how much the water level went up.
w: Volume of nugget = 30.0 mL − 20.0 mL = 10.0 mL. Density = 193 g ÷ 10.0 mL = 19.3 g/mL, which matches gold. The subtraction keeps the tenths place, so 10.0 mL has three significant figures, and so does the answer.

q: Ethanol (0.789 g/mL), vegetable oil (0.92 g/mL) and corn syrup (1.37 g/mL) are compared. A plastic bead has a density of 0.85 g/mL. In which liquids does the bead float?
y: Correct: 0.85 g/mL is less than 0.92 and 1.37 g/mL, so it floats in both, but it is denser than ethanol, so it sinks there.
The bead is denser than ethanol (0.85 > 0.789), so it sinks in ethanol.
It sinks in ethanol, which is less dense than the bead.
It also floats in vegetable oil (0.85 < 0.92).
h: An object floats in any liquid that is denser than it is.
w: Compare 0.85 g/mL with each liquid: ethanol 0.789 (bead denser, sinks), oil 0.92 (bead less dense, floats), syrup 1.37 (floats).

q: A low-dose tablet contains 0.00068 g of active ingredient. Which shows this mass in scientific notation?
y: Correct: the decimal point moves 4 places right to give 6.8, and a value below 1 needs a negative exponent.
A positive exponent would make this 68,000 g, a mass far too large for one tablet.
The decimal point has to pass four digits (0, 0, 0, 6) to land after the 6, not three.
The value is equal, but the coefficient 68 is not between 1 and 10, so it is not proper scientific notation.
h: Move the decimal point until exactly one nonzero digit is in front of it. Count the moves.
w: 0.00068 → 6.8 takes 4 moves to the right, so the mass is 6.8 × 10−4 g.

q: Write 3.92 × 10<sup>−2</sup> L as an ordinary number.
y: Correct: an exponent of −2 moves the decimal point two places to the left.
A negative exponent makes the number smaller than the coefficient; this moved the decimal point the wrong way.
This moves the decimal point only one place left.
This moves the decimal point three places left; the exponent is −2.
h: A negative exponent means a number less than the coefficient. Move the decimal point left that many places.

q: Which pair correctly matches a quantity with its SI base unit?
y: Correct: the kelvin is the SI base unit of temperature.
The liter is a derived unit (1 L = 1 dm<sup>3</sup>); volume has no base unit of its own.
The SI base unit of mass is the kilogram, not the gram.
The SI base unit of length is the meter; the centimeter carries a prefix.
h: The five base units used in this course: meter, kilogram, second, kelvin, mole.
w: Temperature: kelvin. The others: length uses the meter, mass the kilogram, and volume is derived from length (the liter is a cubic decimeter).

q: Which list puts the prefixes in order from smallest to largest?
y: Correct: 10<sup>−6</sup> < 10<sup>−3</sup> < 10<sup>−2</sup> < 10<sup>3</sup>.
Milli- (10<sup>−3</sup>) is a thousand times larger than micro- (10<sup>−6</sup>), so it cannot come first.
This list runs from largest to smallest among the small prefixes; centi- (10<sup>−2</sup>) is the largest of those three.
This list is in order from largest to smallest, the reverse of what was asked.
h: Write each prefix as a power of ten, then compare the exponents.
w: micro- (10−6) < milli- (10−3) < centi- (10−2) < kilo- (103). micro-, milli-, centi-, kilo-.

q: How many milligrams are in 1 kilogram?
y: Correct: 1 kg = 10<sup>3</sup> g and 1 g = 10<sup>3</sup> mg, so 1 kg = 10<sup>3</sup> × 10<sup>3</sup> = 10<sup>6</sup> mg.
10<sup>3</sup> mg is only one gram; a kilogram is a thousand grams.
A kilogram is much larger than a milligram, so it must hold many milligrams, not a tiny fraction of one.
This adds 3 and 2; the two steps are each a factor of 10<sup>3</sup>, so the exponents add to 6.
h: Go through grams: kg → g → mg.
w: 1 kg × (1000 g / 1 kg) × (1000 mg / 1 g) = 106 mg.

q: A food-safety lab finds 1.5 × 10<sup>8</sup> colony-forming units (CFU) per milliliter in a sample, and plates 4.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mL of it. How many CFU are on the plate?
y: Correct: 1.5 × 4.0 = 6.0, and 8 + (−3) = 5.
This adds 8 and 3 and ignores the negative sign on the −3 exponent.
This multiplies the exponents; multiplying powers of ten means adding exponents.
This adds the coefficients (1.5 + 4.0) instead of multiplying them.
h: CFU/mL × mL gives CFU. Multiply coefficients and add exponents, keeping track of signs.
w: (1.5 × 108 CFU/mL)(4.0 × 10−3 mL) = 6.0 × 108 + (−3) = 6.0 × 105 CFU.

q: Calculate (9.0 × 10<sup>−6</sup>) ÷ (3.0 × 10<sup>−2</sup>).
y: Correct: 9.0 ÷ 3.0 = 3.0, and −6 − (−2) = −4.
This adds the exponents, which is the rule for multiplication, not division.
This subtracts in the wrong order (−2 − (−6)); always subtract the bottom exponent from the top one.
This divides the second number by the first, so the fraction is upside down.
h: For division: divide the coefficients and subtract the bottom exponent from the top exponent.
w: (9.0 ÷ 3.0) × 10−6 − (−2) = 3.0 × 10−4.

q: How many significant figures are in each measurement: 500 mg, 500. mg, 5.00 × 10<sup>2</sup> mg?
y: Correct: with no decimal point the zeros in 500 are placeholders; a decimal point or scientific notation makes them count.
500 written without a decimal point has only one significant figure; its trailing zeros do not count.
The decimal point in 500. makes both trailing zeros significant, so it has three.
500. has only three digits, so it cannot have four significant figures.
h: Trailing zeros count only when the number shows a decimal point (or is written in scientific notation).
w: 500 mg → 1; 500. mg → 3 (the decimal point makes the zeros significant); 5.00 × 102 mg → 3.

q: Round 14.0550 to three significant figures.
y: Correct: the third significant digit is the 0 after the decimal point, and the next digit is 5, so it rounds up to 14.1.
The first dropped digit is 5, so the 0 rounds up; keeping 14.0 rounds down.
This keeps four significant figures.
This keeps only two significant figures.
h: Find the third significant digit, then look at the very next digit.
w: Digits 1, 4, 0 | 550. The first dropped digit is 5, so the 0 rounds up: 14.1.

q: Math practice only; always follow the order and facility policy. An infusion pump runs at 83.3 mL/h for a measured 2.5 h. How much volume is delivered, to the correct number of significant figures?
y: Correct: 83.3 × 2.5 = 208.25, and the measured 2.5 h has only two significant figures, so the answer has two.
This keeps three significant figures, but 2.5 h has only two.
This keeps every calculator digit.
This divides the rate by the time; volume delivered is rate × time.
h: In multiplication, the answer has as many significant figures as the value with the fewest.
w: 83.3 mL/h × 2.5 h = 208.25 mL → two significant figures → 2.1 × 102 mL. Writing 210 mL would also show two significant figures under this book's rule, but scientific notation is clearest.

q: A beaker plus a sample has a mass of 52.375 g. The empty beaker, weighed on a different balance, has a mass of 48.2 g. What is the mass of the sample?
y: Correct: 52.375 − 48.2 = 4.175, and subtraction keeps the decimal places of the least precise value (tenths), giving 4.2 g.
This keeps every calculator digit; 48.2 g is known only to the tenths place.
This keeps hundredths, but 48.2 g has only one decimal place.
This rounds to the ones place, losing a digit the data support.
h: For subtraction, count decimal places, not significant figures.
w: 52.375 g − 48.2 g = 4.175 g. The least precise value has one decimal place, so round to tenths: 4.2 g.

q: Calculate (12.50 + 0.6) ÷ 4.385 and report the answer to the correct number of significant figures.
y: Correct: 12.50 + 0.6 = 13.1 (tenths place, three significant figures), and 13.1 ÷ 4.385 = 2.987, which rounds to 2.99.
This keeps four significant figures; the sum 13.1 has only three.
This uses the one significant figure of 0.6 for the whole problem; the addition rule gives a sum with three significant figures.
This divides 0.6 by 4.385 first and then adds; the parentheses mean the addition comes first.
h: Do the part in parentheses first, apply the addition rule, then the division rule.
w: Step 1: 12.50 + 0.6 = 13.10 → 13.1 (tenths place). Step 2: 13.1 ÷ 4.385 = 2.9875… → three significant figures → 2.99.

q: A clinic checks its scale with a 50.0 kg calibration mass. Three readings are 51.8 kg, 51.9 kg and 51.8 kg. Which statement is correct?
c: The scale is precise but not accurate.
The scale is accurate but not precise.
The scale is accurate and precise.
The scale is neither accurate nor precise.
y: Correct: the readings agree within 0.1 kg (precise) but are all about 1.8 kg too high (not accurate).
The readings are close together, so the scale is precise; they are also far from 50.0 kg, so it is not accurate.
Accurate means close to the true 50.0 kg; every reading is almost 2 kg too high.
Readings that agree within 0.1 kg are precise, even though they miss the true value.
h: Precise: do the readings agree with each other? Accurate: are they close to 50.0 kg?
w: The readings agree closely (precise) but average 51.8 kg, about 1.8 kg above the true mass (not accurate). A steady offset like this is a systematic error; recalibrating the scale fixes it.

q: Which equality is not exact, so its digits can limit the significant figures of a result?
y: Correct: 2.205 is a rounded value (the true factor has more digits), so it carries four significant figures.
The inch is defined as exactly 2.54 cm, so this factor is exact.
Metric prefixes are definitions, so 1 km = 1000 m is exact.
An hour is defined as 60 minutes, so this factor is exact.
h: Exact factors are definitions. Which factor is a rounded measurement between two systems?
w: 1 kg = 2.205 lb is rounded to four significant figures. Definitions (1 km = 1000 m, 1 h = 60 min) and the defined 1 in = 2.54 cm are exact and never limit a result.

q: Math practice only; always follow the order and facility policy. An order is for 0.10 mg/kg. The patient weighs 165 lb. Using 1 kg = 2.205 lb, what dose in milligrams does the order describe?
y: Correct: 165 lb ÷ 2.205 lb/kg = 74.83 kg, and 74.83 kg × 0.10 mg/kg = 7.5 mg (two significant figures).
This multiplies the weight in pounds by 0.10 mg/kg; convert pounds to kilograms first.
This multiplies by 2.205 instead of dividing, so the weight in kilograms came out larger than in pounds.
The arithmetic is right, but 0.10 mg/kg has only two significant figures.
h: Pounds → kilograms first (the number gets smaller), then multiply by mg/kg.
w: 165 lb × (1 kg / 2.205 lb) = 74.83 kg; × (0.10 mg / 1 kg) = 7.483 mg → 7.5 mg.

q: Math practice only; always follow the order and facility policy. A 1.00 L bag of normal saline is ordered to run over 8.0 h. What is the rate in mL/h?
y: Correct: 1000 mL ÷ 8.0 h = 125 mL/h, and 8.0 h has two significant figures, so the rate is 1.3 × 10<sup>2</sup> mL/h.
The arithmetic is right, but the 8.0 h limits the answer to two significant figures.
This divides 1.00 L by 8.0 h without changing liters to milliliters.
This multiplies volume by time; a rate is volume divided by time.
h: Change L to mL, then divide by the hours.
w: 1.00 L × (1000 mL / 1 L) ÷ 8.0 h = 125 mL/h → two significant figures → 1.3 × 102 mL/h. (In practice, pump settings follow the order and policy; this is a significant-figure exercise.)

q: A skin graft has an area of 2.5 in<sup>2</sup>. What is the area in cm<sup>2</sup>? (1 in = 2.54 cm exactly)
y: Correct: (2.54 cm/in)<sup>2</sup> = 6.4516 cm<sup>2</sup>/in<sup>2</sup>, and 2.5 × 6.4516 = 16.129, which rounds to 16 cm<sup>2</sup>.
This uses 2.54 only once; for square inches the factor must be squared.
This divides by the squared factor; a square centimeter is smaller than a square inch, so the number should get larger.
This keeps four significant figures; 2.5 in<sup>2</sup> has two.
h: Square the whole conversion factor: (2.54 cm / 1 in)<sup>2</sup>.
w: 2.5 in2 × (2.54 cm / 1 in)2 = 2.5 × 6.4516 cm2 = 16.129 cm2 → 16 cm2.

q: A CT scan estimates the volume of a bone graft as 3.5 × 10<sup>4</sup> mm<sup>3</sup>. What is the volume in milliliters? (1 cm = 10 mm; 1 cm<sup>3</sup> = 1 mL)
y: Correct: (1 cm/10 mm)<sup>3</sup> = 1 cm<sup>3</sup> per 1000 mm<sup>3</sup>, so 3.5 × 10<sup>4</sup> mm<sup>3</sup> = 35 cm<sup>3</sup> = 35 mL.
This divides by 10 only once; a cubic unit needs the factor cubed (1000).
This multiplies by 1000; a cubic centimeter is larger than a cubic millimeter, so the number should get smaller.
This divides by 10<sup>6</sup>, the factor between mm<sup>3</sup> and L (or between cm<sup>3</sup> and m<sup>3</sup>), not between mm<sup>3</sup> and cm<sup>3</sup>.
h: 1 cm<sup>3</sup> is a cube 10 mm on each side: 10 × 10 × 10 mm<sup>3</sup>.
w: 3.5 × 104 mm3 × (1 cm / 10 mm)3 = 3.5 × 104 ÷ 103 cm3 = 35 cm3 = 35 mL.

q: A lab needs 150. g of isopropyl alcohol (density 0.786 g/mL). What volume should be measured?
y: Correct: 150. g × (1 mL / 0.786 g) = 190.8 mL, which rounds to three significant figures as 191 mL.
This multiplies mass by density; the grams do not cancel that way.
This divides the density by the mass, which gives the wrong units and a tiny number.
This keeps four significant figures; 150. g and 0.786 g/mL each have three.
h: Use the density upside down (1 mL / 0.786 g) so grams cancel.
w: 150. g × (1 mL / 0.786 g) = 190.8 mL → 191 mL. Check: the alcohol is less dense than water, so 150. g takes up more than 150 mL.

q: A Valley dairy's bulk tank holds 5.00 × 10<sup>3</sup> L of milk (density 1.03 g/mL). What is the mass of the milk in kilograms?
y: Correct: 5.00 × 10<sup>6</sup> mL × 1.03 g/mL = 5.15 × 10<sup>6</sup> g = 5.15 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg.
This skips the L → mL step, so the answer is 1000 times too small.
This divides by the density instead of multiplying.
This stops at grams and labels the result kilograms.
h: Chain: L → mL → g (density) → kg.
w: 5.00 × 103 L × (1000 mL / 1 L) × (1.03 g / 1 mL) × (1 kg / 1000 g) = 5.15 × 103 kg. Check: milk is slightly denser than water, so the kilograms slightly exceed the liters.
